pr_title: Feature: verify the authenticity of a webhook event
pr_body:
Fixes #11819 

---

When Spree sends a webhook event to a webhook subscriber, there is no way for the webhook subscriber to verify the authenticity of the webhook event. Due to this, a webhook subscriber needs to allow only certain IP-addresses to be sure the webhook event is actually coming from a verified source.

This PR adds support for an event signature (based on the subscriber's `secret_key` and the payload), so the webhook subscriber can verify the authenticity of the source of the event.

The event signature is added as an HTTP request header (`X-Spree-Hmac-SHA256` or `HTTP_X_SPREE_HMAC_SHA256` for PHP, or a Rack-based framework such as Ruby on Rails or Sinatra) for every request send to the webhook subscriber. 

**It's up to the webhook subscriber to implement the verification of the authenticity.**

Hereby an example (taken from Shopify's documentation):

```ruby
# The following example uses Ruby and the Sinatra web framework to verify a webhook request:
require 'rubygems'
require 'base64'
require 'openssl'
require 'sinatra'
require 'active_support/security_utils'

# The webhook secret key is viewable from the Spree Backend Dashboard. 
# In a production environment, it's recommended to set the client secret as an environment variable to prevent exposing it in code.
CLIENT_SECRET = 'my_client_secret'

helpers do
  # Compare the computed HMAC digest based on the client secret and the request contents to the reported HMAC in the headers
  def verify_webhook(data, hmac_header)
    calculated_hmac = Base64.strict_encode64(OpenSSL::HMAC.digest('sha256', CLIENT_SECRET, data))
    ActiveSupport::SecurityUtils.secure_compare(calculated_hmac, hmac_header)
  end
end

# Respond to HTTP POST requests sent to this web service
post '/' do
  request.body.rewind
  data = request.body.read
  verified = verify_webhook(data, env["HTTP_X_SPREE_HMAC_SHA256"])

  halt 401 unless verified

  # Process webhook payload
  # ...
end
```

Feedback I'm looking for:

- Is the addition of event's signature in the `Spree::Webhooks::Subscribers::MakeRequest` implemented in a way that is conform the code style of the Spree project?
- The chosen name of the HTTP header is `X-Spree-Hmac-SHA256`. Do you feel this is a suiting name?
- The visibility of the `WebhookSubscriber#secret_key` in the admin dashboard isn't implemented yet as I wanted to do that in a separate PR. Do you agree?

I haven't updated the documentation (`spree-dev-docs`) yet, but I also noticed there is no documentation yet for the webhooks. Is any help needed on that front?

Looking forward to your feedback. Merry Christmas 🎄

Agree, name sounds good to me 👍

Just a thought - we could also opt for a more generic header, i.e. one that does not contain a specific hash function in the name? AFAIR Shopify uses `X-Shopify-Hmac-SHA256` and Slack `X-Slack-Signature` so both are used in the wild. I guess the advantage is that the name is decoupled from the hash function which might have some pros and cons. That being said, I'm okay with the proposed name.

On a different note - we should probably also include the timestamp in a header, e.g. `X-Spree-Timestamp`/`X-Spree-Request-Timestamp`, and also include it in the signature. This will prevent events from being valid forever.
@kshalot +1 for including a timestamp - not necessarily as a part of this PR, but it's a common practice that goes along with request signatures.

issue_context.title: Verifying the webhook event's authenticity
issue_context.body:
# Problem

Currently, the webhook events fired by Spree to third-party applications or internal applications are lacking a message signature. Due to this, you're unable to verify whether Spree is actually the application sending events to the webhook subscription API endpoints.

When bad actors are able to find the endpoints, they're able to send malformed data to these endpoints. As third-party services or internal applications are taking the authenticity for granted without verifying the IP (for example) it could lead to problems.

# Solution

There are multiple ways to protect yourself against these kinds of attacks. One would be to verify the IP address of the machine sending the webhook event. However, sometimes this might not be a feasible solution.

Another one could be to include a message signature based on a base64-encoded HMAC SHA256 signature. The message signature is generated using the webhook secret key that will be generated upon creation of the webhook subscription (`Spree::WebhookSubscriber`).

The receiver of the webhook event can then compute the HMAC digest with the webhook secret from the webhook subscription and thereby verify the authenticity of the webhook event.

# Alternatives

As pointed out before, one can also protect the webhook subscription API endpoints based on the IP address of the message sender. However, I'd argue that Spree should provide the tools also when blocking out requests based on IP address isn't feasible.

# Implementation steps

1. Generate a (readable) secret key for every webhook subscriber (`Spree::WebhookSubscriber`) before creating.
2. Add a new data model called `Spree::Webhook::EventSignature` which can build a base64-encoded HMAC SHA256 signature for a specific event and webhook subscriber.
3. Add the event signature to the headers of the HTTP request to the webhook API subscription endpoints.

# Additional resources

The documentation of Shopify includes a great example of how the verification of the event's authenticity could look like from the point of view of a webhook subscriber; https://shopify.dev/apps/webhooks/configuration/https#step-5-verify-the-webhook

I would be more than happy to take a stab at this and do the implementation for it. However, before doing so, I'd be interested to learn if the core team would also consider this a valuable feature.

review_comments:
I think `OpenSSL::HMAC.digest('sha256', @event.subscriber.secret_key, payload)` will fail when the key parameter is `nil`. I'd suggest adding two more migrations as a part of this PR:
1. A migration that will generate and backfill empty secret_keys for spree_webhooks_subscribers
2. A migration that will disallow nulls in the secret_key column

This way we'll make sure we won't break any webhook subscribers in existing installations of Spree
Thank you! I'll add these migrations. As I said before, I wasn't fully aware of how the Spree core team likes to handle these kinds of migrations. I'll make the adjustments.
